title: 'The Extasie': title and tradition
short: Ecstasy: the soul's going out of the body in rapture; Donne applies the mystical and Neoplatonic idea to two lovers.
body: 'Ecstasy' (Greek ekstasis) meant the departure of the soul from the body in trance or rapture, as in St Paul's being caught up 'whether in the body, or out of the body, I cannot tell' (2 Corinthians 12:2-3), in Plotinus, and in Aquinas. Grierson called the poem one of Donne's most important statements of the interdependence of body and soul, and noted that Donne in a letter compares serious letter-writing to ecstasy. Lord Herbert of Cherbury's 'Ode upon a Question moved, Whether Love should continue for ever' appears to imitate it. First printed 1633.

title: A Pregnant banke ... violets
short: A swelling bank like a pillow, with a drooping violet: a fertile pastoral setting with discreet sexual suggestion.
body: The opening places the lovers in a pastoral landscape with erotic overtones: the 'pregnant' bank swells like a pillow on a bed, and the violet reclines its head. The violet was an emblem of love and faithfulness. Readers who take the poem as seduction see the setting as preparing for the bodily conclusion; others read it as the natural fertility that the poem's argument eventually sanctifies. The violet returns in ll. 37-40.

title: cimented / With a fast balme
short: Their clasped hands are glued together by a 'balm', their perspiration, imagined as a precious, preserving fluid.
body: 'Balm' was an aromatic resin and, in Paracelsian medicine, a vital preservative essence in the body. Here it is the moisture of the joined palms, 'fast' because it binds firmly. In Elizabethan love-lore a moist palm signified amorousness (compare Othello III.iv). The hands are 'cimented' (cemented): the first of a series of images of joining (thread, graft, knot) that culminate in the 'subtile knot' of l. 64.

title: eye-beames twisted ... one double string
short: Following the old 'extramission' theory of sight, beams from each lover's eyes meet and twist into one thread.
body: Many ancient and Renaissance writers held that sight works by rays sent out from the eye. Donne literalises the idea: the lovers' eye-beams twist together and thread their eyes on a single double string, like beads. The image is both precise and slightly grotesque, typical of what Samuel Johnson called the metaphysical poets' yoking of heterogeneous ideas. The 'double string' prepares for the idea of two souls made one.

title: entergraft
short: To graft into one another, as gardeners graft scions: Grierson prefers 'entergraft' to 'engraft' because only it gives reciprocity.
body: Grafting joins a shoot of one plant to another so that they grow as one. Grierson notes that 'entergraft' (inter-graft) has the best manuscript support and alone conveys the mutual sense: each hand grafted into the other. The horticultural image anticipates the violet transplanted in l. 37. Grafting was also a familiar figure for marriage and for the union of two families, so the word hints at a lasting bond. The elision mark in 'to'entergraft' shows that the two syllables are run together to keep the four-stress line.

anchor: pictures in our eyes to get
title: pictures in our eyes ... propagation
short: Their only 'offspring' so far are the tiny images of each other reflected in their eyes ('looking babies').
body: To 'get' meant to beget. The reflections of each lover in the other's pupils, popularly 'babies in the eyes', are wittily called their only 'propagation'. The joke implies a sexual union not yet made, and so raises the question the poem must answer: whether their union is to remain purely spiritual. Compare 'The Good-morrow', l. 15. 'All the meanes' and 'all our propagation' stress how little, so far, the bodies have done.

title: Our soules ... were gone out
short: Like Fate hovering between two armies, the lovers' souls have left their bodies and hang in the space between them.
body: This is the ecstasy proper: the souls leave their bodies 'to advance their state' (to improve their condition, and in diplomatic language to promote their interests) and hang between the lovers like Fate suspending victory over two evenly matched armies. The military simile gives way in l. 17 to diplomatic 'negotiation', a characteristic Donne mixture of public and private vocabulary.

title: sepulchrall statues
short: The soulless bodies lie still like stone effigies on a tomb, silent all day.
body: Recumbent effigies on Tudor and Jacobean tombs, often of husband and wife side by side, are the model. The comparison stresses that the bodies are now empty, as if dead. Grierson cites Pascal on the eloquence of lovers' silence for l. 20. The repetition 'All day ... all the day' slows the verse to match the stillness. The tomb image also hints at death, which the poem later answers with the bodies' return to life.

title: concoction
short: A refining by heat, in alchemy or digestion: an ideal observer would be further purified by overhearing the lovers' souls.
body: The imagined bystander, 'by love refin'd' and grown 'all minde', could understand the souls' wordless language. He would take 'a new concoction': in alchemy and physiology, concoction was the process of maturing or refining by heat, as food is 'concocted' into blood. He would leave purer than he came. The figure introduces the idea, completed at the end, of the lovers as an example to others.

title: it was not sexe
short: The ecstasy shows them that what drew them was not sex; they had not understood what moved them.
body: The ecstasy 'unperplexes' (clarifies) their love: they now see that its source was the soul, not bodily desire. Grierson explains that the lovers perceive their attraction to have been spiritual in origin. 'Sexe' here may mean sexual difference as well as desire. The phrase bears on the larger debate: the poem first denies that sex was the motive and then argues for a return to the body.

title: Mixture of things ... each this and that
short: Every soul is a mixture of unknown elements; love re-mixes two souls into one, so each is both itself and the other.
body: Renaissance theorists debated whether souls were simple or compounded. Donne takes them as mixtures, then makes love an alchemist that mixes two souls again to produce one compound in which 'each [is] this and that'. Helen Gardner related the poem's argument to Leone Ebreo's Dialoghi d'amore (1535), where lovers' souls are united yet need the body; others point to Ficino and the wider Florentine Neoplatonic tradition.

title: A single violet transplant
short: A transplanted violet doubles and multiplies in strength and colour; so a soul joined by love to another grows richer.
body: Gardeners believed that transplanting improved a plant. The violet, picked up from the opening landscape, now becomes an emblem of the new, double soul; 'redoubles' and 'multiplies' also hint at propagation. The image extends the grafting of l. 9. 'Still' means continually: the transplanted flower goes on increasing. The point of the analogy is that the soul, like the plant, gains from being moved out of its single state and set in a new soil, that is, joined with another soul. The 'scant' violet becomes abundant.

title: Interanimates
short: Love gives each soul life from the other; the resulting 'abler soule' overcomes ('controules') the defects of loneliness.
body: This archive's text reads 'Interanimates', the form of the early editions; Grierson printed 'Interinanimates', with manuscript support, and defended related forms from Donne's sermons. The word means to animate mutually. The 'abler soule' that results is stronger than either alone; 'controules' means overpowers, corrects (compare 'The Good-morrow', l. 10). The 'abler soule' is the speaker's name for the compound soul of the two lovers.

title: Atomies
short: Atoms, the indivisible particles of which things are made; the new soul's atoms are souls, which cannot decay.
body: 'Atomy' (atom) was used of the tiny indivisible particles of Democritean and Epicurean physics, and loosely for any minute particle. The lovers' new soul is built not of physical atoms, which decay as compounds change, but of souls, which are immune to change. The argument parallels the scholastic premise of 'The Good-morrow', l. 19. The lovers thus claim for their joint soul the immortality that philosophy granted to the simple soul.

title: Wee are / The intelligences, they the spheares
short: The souls are like the angelic intelligences that move the heavenly spheres; the bodies are the spheres they guide.
body: The turn at 'But O alas' asks why they keep apart from their bodies. The answer adapts Ptolemaic cosmology, in which each sphere is moved by an intelligence: the bodies are 'ours, though not wee', instruments that the soul governs. Grierson notes that all the manuscripts read the singular 'spheare' (the early editions print the plural), and he kept it. The same image appears in 'Aire and Angels'.

title: drosse ... allay
short: The bodies are not dross (waste) but alloy, the baser metal that strengthens gold for use.
body: Metallurgy: dross is the scum thrown off in smelting; alloy ('allay') is the base metal mixed with gold or silver to make it hard enough for coinage. The body, then, is a necessary admixture, not refuse. The bodies first 'convay' (conveyed, introduced) the lovers to each other and yielded their senses' force. This archive reads 'senses force' with 1633; Grierson emended to 'forces, sense', which he thought the harder, more characteristic reading.

title: heavens influence ... imprints the ayre
short: Astrological influence reaches man through the air, so soul reaches soul through the body. 'For soule' here; Grierson emended to 'Soe soule'.
body: Astrology held that the stars act on man through the medium of the air; Grierson illustrates from Du Bartas. The analogy: just as heaven's influence must first 'imprint' the air, so one soul must pass through the body to reach another. This text reads 'For soule' (1633); Grierson emended to 'Soe soule', citing Aquinas on the heavenly intelligences, and later editors are divided. With 'For', the lines read as a reason; with 'Soe', as the second term of an analogy.

title: Spirits ... that subtile knot
short: Renaissance physiology: the blood produces 'spirits', fine vapours that tie the soul to the body and so make us human.
body: Physicians taught that the blood produced 'spirits' (natural, vital and animal), very fine substances that served as the link between the immaterial soul and the body. Grierson quotes Burton's Anatomy of Melancholy and a Donne sermon on the spirits as the knot binding soul and body. The 'subtile knot' (fine, delicate) 'makes us man': a human being is neither soul nor body alone but their union.

title: a great Prince in prison
short: Unless the soul descends to the senses and faculties, it is like a king locked up, unable to act.
body: Pure souls must 'descend' to the affections (emotions) and faculties that the senses can reach; otherwise the soul is a prince imprisoned. The image reverses the Platonic commonplace of the body as the soul's prison (Phaedo; compare Marvell's 'Dialogue between the Soul and Body'): here the soul is imprisoned if it is cut off from the body. Gardner took this as the heart of the poem's serious argument about the incarnate nature of human love.

title: the body is his booke
short: Love's mysteries grow in souls, but the body is the book in which ordinary people can read them.
body: 'Mysteries' carries a religious sense (the sacraments, revealed truths), and 'love reveal'd' parallels revealed religion. As Scripture is the book in which weak men read God, so the body is the book in which love can be read. The lines justify the return to the bodies as both natural and exemplary. Critics who read the poem as seduction see the theology as specious; others take it as Donne's serious incarnational view of love.

title: this dialogue of one
short: The two souls' conversation is really one voice; an ideal witness would see little change when they return to their bodies.
body: The poem ends by recalling the observer of ll. 21-28: if some lover like them has 'heard' this 'dialogue of one' (two souls speaking as one), he will see 'small change' when they are 'to bodies gone'. Whether 'small change' means that bodily love will preserve the spiritual union, or archly understates what is about to happen, is one of the cruxes on which the reading of the whole poem depends.

title: Philosophy or seduction?
short: Critics have long disputed whether the poem is a serious account of love's union of soul and body or an elaborate seduction argument.
body: Grierson read the poem as a serious statement of the interdependence of soul and body. Pierre Legouis (Donne the Craftsman, 1928) argued that it is a dramatised seduction in which Neoplatonic language serves physical ends. Helen Gardner's 'The Argument about "The Ecstasy"' (1959) answered Legouis, linking the poem to Leone Ebreo and stressing that its 'we' is shared by both lovers, so there is no one to seduce. A 2004 essay in SEL argues that the seduction reading, later dominant, misses a tradition of 'voluptuous rationalism' behind the poem. Students should notice that the speaker reports what 'we said' together, which supports Gardner, while the setting and witty logic support Legouis.

anchor: Sat we two, one anothers best
title: Form
short: Seventy-six lines of iambic tetrameter in quatrains rhyming abab, printed continuously.
body: The short four-stress line and alternate rhymes give the poem the movement of a steady argument; its length is unusual for the Songs and Sonets. The quatrain units are clear even though the text is printed as one block: each quatrain usually completes a step in the reasoning, with longer syntactic periods across ll. 21-28 and 61-68 where the argument is most intricate. Ll. 1-4 complete the opening sentence: the lovers sat on the bank, 'one anothers best'.
